source.title: Generalization in Learning: Eyring Formula and Predator-prey Model
source.authors: S. V. Kozyrev; I. A. Lopatin; A. N. Pechen

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. The text gives 2026 dates while the supplied venue metadata gives 2025.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses grokking and proposes a thermodynamic explanation, but reports no new grokking experiment. Its own experiment concerns overfitting in polynomial regression and does not test a listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The account of grokking in Section 3, including the timing and training-set-size findings, is a summary of cited work [7], not a result of this study. The authors' own numerical results concern polynomial regression with a predator-prey method.
record.test_reason: Section 3 offers a thermodynamic (Eyring-formula, Brownian-motion-on-zero-risk-manifold) explanation of grokking, but every grokking fact it uses is recapped from Power et al. [7], one of the original sources. The only experiment (Section 5) is polynomial regression of noisy sin(πx) comparing gradient descent with a predator-prey optimizer. It reports no delayed-generalization curve, no circuit or progress measures, no weight-norm or initialization control, no LLM run and no optimizer or precision ablation. The theory does not argue that any version is wrong, so it is not T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct; add the content of the grokking argument. The authors claim thermodynamic arguments explain grokking: fast memorization as drift to a zero-risk manifold, then slow Brownian motion along it, with the Eyring formula giving exponential dependence of grokking time on sample size. They also claim the predator-prey method reduced overfitting in one polynomial-regression example. The grokking part is argument only, with no new data.
record.recipe_differences: No grokking experiment is performed. The paper gives a theoretical discussion and separately runs a predator-prey regression simulation.
record.method_sensitivity: The regression results vary with polynomial degree; the authors identify degree 1 as underfitting, degree 3 as normal learning, and degrees 5 and 7 as overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: In noisy sin(πx) polynomial regression (likely d=5), the predator-prey optimizer lowers the best test MSE over the last N iterations from 0.161 to 0.106. It also lowers deviation from the hidden function from 0.0594 to 0.0334, compared with gradient descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A predator-prey optimizer that pushes parameters out of narrow minima reduces overfitting in small regression problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Theoretical proposal: memorization is drift toward the zero-risk manifold (distance ∝ t). Generalization is zero-gradient Brownian motion along it toward high entropy (distance ∝ √t). The Eyring formula then predicts grokking time rising exponentially as the training set shrinks. No experiment is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay is an entropic barrier-crossing time on the zero-risk manifold, rising exponentially as the training set shrinks.

record.problems: The grokking discussion summarizes cited work rather than providing a new test. The paper reports a numerical example for one regression problem; the predator-prey comparison does not state the polynomial degree in the comparison text, and its plotted trajectories have no numeric values. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Delayed jump in test accuracy and its growth as the training set shrinks. These are only recapped from [7] and given a theoretical Eyring-formula account; there is no new measurement.
Gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, progress measures. The proposed alternative (entropic Brownian drift along the zero-risk manifold) is not measured.
Grokking on non-algorithmic data; lazy-to-rich switching via initialization scale or weight norm. The regression experiment shows no grokking-like delay.
Weight-decay efficiency, critical dataset size, ungrokking. None are tested; the paper only notes from [7] that regularization helps.
All parts; no cross-run algorithm comparison.
All parts; no optimizer or floating-point controls.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not itself an original source, but its grokking section relies entirely on one (arXiv:2201.02177). The √t versus t argument rests on the recapped 10^3 versus 10^6 step figures from [7]. Rows r13–r16 are the study's own method compared with gradient descent and should not count as phenomenon rows. Dates in the text (2026) conflict with the venue metadata (2025).

versions.untested_parts: No new test of the delayed test-performance rise or how its delay varies with training-set size; Section 3 only recaps cited findings.
The paper proposes Brownian motion along a zero-risk manifold as an explanation, but does not measure circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or progress measures.
The regression experiment is non-algorithmic, but it does not test grokking-like delays or initialization-scale/weight-norm control.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking result is tested.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs is reported.
No optimizer-instability or floating-point artifact control is tested.
